l: second war against Thebes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having spoke suflBciently of these things, we shall now proceed
s: The second war against Thebes was undertaken by the Epigoni to avenge their fathers' deaths. The Epigoni defeated the Thebans, who abandoned the city, after which the city was entered and razed.

l: Tiresias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having spoke suflBciently of these things, we shall now proceed
s: Tiresias advised the defeated Thebans to abandon Thebes as the only means of preserving themselves. He later died at Tilphossus and was buried by the Cadmeans with great funeral pomp, after which he was worshiped as a god.

l: Cadmeans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having spoke suflBciently of these things, we shall now proceed
s: The Cadmeans followed Tiresias's advice and fled Thebes at night to Tilphossus. They later buried Tiresias, and in time they invaded the Dorians, expelled them, and settled in their country before some returned to Thebes and the rest remained in Doria.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: This unit recounts the legendary origins and descendants of the Aeolians, including Arne, Aeolus, Boeotus, Salmoneus, Tyro, Pelias, Neleus, and Nestor. It describes the Lapiths and Centaurs, the conflict between them, and the ancestry of Lapithus, Ixion, Perithous, and Hippodamia. It also follows Asclepius and his sons, the daughters of Asopus and the sons of Aeacus, including Peleus, Telamon, Achilles, and Ajax. Finally, it recounts the stories of Pelops, Tantalus, Oenomaus, Hippodamia, and the Trojan royal line from Ilus and Tros to Priam and Hector.

l: Aeolians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: The Aeolians are described through traditions concerning the descendants of Aeolus. Their history includes the settlement of Aeolus at the Aeolian Islands and the later origins of the Boeotians.

l: Aeolus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Aeolus was descended from Deucalion and Helen. Another Aeolus, descended from Mimas, fathered Arne; after Arne bore Aeolus and Boeotus, he rejected her and delivered her to a Metapontian stranger.

l: Arne, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Arne, the daughter of Aeolus, bore Aeolus and Boeotus by Neptune. She was sent to Metapontum, later fled with her sons after a quarrel, and accompanied them to the Aeolian Islands.

l: Neptune, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Neptune fathered Boeotus by Arne and Pelias and Neleus by Tyro. He also carried Cercyra and Salamis away to the islands later named after them.

l: Salmoneus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Salmoneus, the son of Helen and nephew of Aeolus, established himself in Elis and founded the city of Salmone. He was cruel and impious, and Jupiter killed him with a thunderbolt.

l: Tyro, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Tyro was the beautiful daughter of Salmoneus. Neptune fathered Pelias and Neleus by her, and after she married Cretheus she had Amythaon, Pheretes, and Aeson.

l: Jupiter Triphylius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: The figure identified in this record as Jupiter struck Salmoneus and Asclepius with thunderbolts. He also purified Ixion after Ixion killed Hesioneus, and by Aegina fathered Aeacus.

l: Pelias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Pelias was the son of Neptune and Tyro and later the son of Cretheus. He reigned at Iolchus and, in conflict with Neleus, led an incursion into the Peloponnese with Melampus and Bias.

l: Neleus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Neleus was the son of Neptune and Tyro. He entered Messenia, founded Pylos, married Chloris, and fathered twelve sons, including Nestor.

l: Melampus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Melampus, a soothsayer and son of Amythaon, restored women of Argos to sanity after they were driven mad by Bacchus. Anaxagoras rewarded him with a third of the kingdom, and he governed Argos with Bias.

l: Pylos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Pylos was the city founded by Neleus in Messenia after the bordering inhabitants gave him the territory.

l: Nestor, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Nestor was the youngest son of Neleus and Chloris. He went with his brothers to the Trojan War and was one of the Grecian commanders.

l: Lapithae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: The Lapiths took their name from Lapithus, who ruled near the river Peneus. Their later conflict with the Centaurs led to many deaths and forced survivors to flee to Pholoe and Malea.

l: centaurs, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: The Centaurs are variously said to have descended from Ixion and a cloud shaped like Juno, or from Nephele and Ixion. They fought the Lapiths, attacked women at the marriage feast of Perithous and Hippodamia, and later raided and killed neighboring inhabitants.

l: Apollo, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Apollo fathered Lapithus and Centaurus by Stilbes. He also killed the Cyclops who made the thunderbolt with which Asclepius was killed, and later killed Niobe’s sons at Latona’s command.

l: Lapithus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Lapithus, descended from Peneus and Stilbes, lived near the river Peneus and ruled the surrounding territory. His sons were Phorbas and Periphas, and the Lapiths took their name from him.

l: Ixion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Ixion married Dia after promising her father Hesioneus a dowry, but failed to fulfill the promise. He killed Hesioneus in a fiery furnace, was purified by Jupiter, pursued Juno, and fathered the Centaurs through a cloud shaped like her; he was later bound to a wheel and tortured.

l: Perithous, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Perithous was the son of Ixion and Dia. He married Hippodamia, invited Theseus and the Centaurs to the wedding, and joined the Lapiths against the drunken Centaurs.

l: Hippodamia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Hippodamia was the daughter of Bystus and the wife of Perithous. Her marriage feast became the occasion for the Centaurs’ attempted assault on the women present.

l: Asclepius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Asclepius was the son of Apollo and Coronis and became famous for discovering medical remedies. Because he restored many apparently dead people, Jupiter killed him with a thunderbolt.

l: Asopus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Asopus dwelt at Phlias and married Medon, by whom he had two sons and twelve daughters. His daughters gave their names to places and peoples, including Aegina, Salamis, and Sinope.

l: Aegina, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Aegina was carried by Jupiter from Phlias to the island that received her name. She bore Aeacus, who later became king of the island.

l: Aeacus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Aeacus was the son of Jupiter and Aegina and later became king of Aegina. His sons were Peleus and Telamon.

l: Peleus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Peleus accidentally killed his half-brother Phocus with a hand stone and was banished by Aeacus. He fled to Phthia, was purified by Actor, succeeded Actor as king, and fathered Achilles by Thetis.

l: Telamon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Telamon fled from Aegina to Salamis and became king there after marrying Glauce, the king’s daughter. After Glauce died, he married Eribna of Athens and fathered Ajax.

l: Achilles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Achilles was the son of Peleus and Thetis. He went with Agamemnon to the Trojan War and killed Memnon.

l: Ajax, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Ajax was the son of Telamon and Eribna of Athens. He was another associate of Agamemnon in the Trojan War.

l: Pelops, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Pelops came to Pisa seeking Hippodamia and bribed Myrtilus to let him win the horse race. He gained Hippodamia and the kingdom of Pisa, then conquered much of the Peloponnese, which was named after him.

l: Tantalus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Tantalus was a rich and renowned son of Jupiter who ruled in the part of Asia later called Phrygia. After revealing the gods’ secrets to men, he was punished during life and condemned to eternal torment after death; he was the father of Pelops and Niobe.

l: Oenomaus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Oenomaus was the son of Mars and Harpina and the father of Hippodamia. Fearing an oracle that he would die when she married, he challenged her suitors to a horse race and killed those who lost; after Pelops won, Oenomaus killed himself.

l: Pisa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Pisa was a city of the Peloponnese where Oenomaus ruled. Pelops won Hippodamia there and gained the kingdom.

l: horse race, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: The horse race ran from Pisa to Neptune’s altar in the isthmus of Corinth. Oenomaus allowed each suitor to start first, then pursued him in a chariot and killed him unless he was overtaken by the suitor.

l: Peloponnesus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: The Peloponnese was largely subdued by Pelops after he gained the kingdom of Pisa. It was named after him.

l: Ilus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Ilus was the son of Tros and expelled Tantalus from Paphlagonia. He founded the city of Ilium in the plain of Troas.

l: Tros, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Tros was the son of Erichthonius and gave his name to the Trojans. His sons were Ilus, Assaracus, and Ganymedes.

l: Troas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Troas was the country ruled first by Teucer and later associated with the descendants of Tros. Ilus founded Ilium in its plain.

l: Trojans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: The Trojans were named after Tros. Their history in this unit includes the rule of Priam, the valor of Hector, and the aid brought by Memnon during the Trojan War.

l: Ilium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Ilium was the city founded by Ilus in the plain of Troas.

l: Priam, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Priam was the son of Laomedon and married Hecuba. Among his many sons was Hector, who was especially distinguished for valor in the Trojan War.

l: Hector, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: Hector was the son of Priam and Hecuba. He was especially remarkable for his valor in the Trojan War.

l: Trojan War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: The Trojan War included the participation of Nestor, Achilles, Ajax, and the sons of Asclepius on the Grecian side. Hector fought with distinction for the Trojans, while Memnon brought aid to Troy and was killed by Achilles.

l: war of the Lapiths and Centaurs, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Here it is necessary to give a distinct and particular accomit of*
s: The war began after the Centaurs, invited to the marriage of Perithous and Hippodamia, became drunk and attempted to ravish the women. Theseus and the Lapiths killed many Centaurs and drove the rest away, after which the Centaurs made war on the Lapiths, killing most of them and forcing the survivors into exile.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The unit concerns Daedalus, his inventions and works in Crete and Sicily, and his escape from Minos after helping Pasiphae approach the bull and building the labyrinth. It recounts Minos's invasion of Sicily and death at the hands of Cocalus, followed by the settlement of Cretans and the building of the temple of the Curetes or Corybantes. It also relates the genealogy and deeds of Aristaeus, the history of Eryx and Venus Erycina's temple, and the story of Daphnis among the Berei Mountains.

l: Daedalus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Daedalus was an Athenian of the family of the Erechthidae and was celebrated for his skill in architecture, statuary, stonework, and the invention of tools. After secretly murdering Talus, he fled to Crete, where he served Minos, helped Pasiphae approach the bull, and built the labyrinth. He later escaped with Icarus and settled in Sicily under the protection of Cocalus, for whom he constructed several notable works.

l: Talus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Talus, Daedalus's sister's son, was trained by Daedalus and surpassed him in ingenuity. He invented the potter's wheel, the saw, the turning lathe, and other architectural tools, but Daedalus secretly murdered him out of jealousy.

l: Crete, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Crete was ruled by Minos and was the place where Daedalus found refuge and favor after fleeing Athens. Daedalus and Icarus escaped from Crete, and the island was also associated with the worship of the Curetes or Corybantes and the concealment of Jupiter from Saturn.

l: Minos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Minos was king of Crete and was said to have dominion at sea. He threatened Daedalus, invaded Sicily to recover him, and died after Cocalus kept him in a hot bath until he was suffocated.

l: Pasiphae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Pasiphae, the wife of Minos, became madly enamored of a bull after Minos failed to sacrifice the finest bull to Neptune. With Daedalus's help, she approached the bull by means of an artificial cow and gave birth to the Minotaur.

l: the Cretan labyrinth, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The labyrinth was built by Daedalus to house and feed the Minotaur. It was full of winding passages and turnings and was impossible for strangers to find their way through; the seven boys and seven girls sent yearly from Athens were consumed there.

l: Icarus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Icarus fled Crete with his father, Daedalus. In one account he fell into the sea while trying to land on an island, and in another he fell when the sun melted the wax holding his artificial wings together; the sea and island were thereafter called Icarian.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Sicily received Daedalus, who worked there under Cocalus, and it was later invaded by Minos. The island was also associated with the Cretans who settled there, Aristaeus's teachings, the temple of Venus at Eryx, and the pastoral traditions connected with Daphnis.

l: Cocalus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Cocalus was the ruler of Sicily who received Daedalus courteously and made him his close friend. He protected Daedalus from Minos and caused Minos to be suffocated in a hot bath, afterward presenting his body to the Cretans as though he had accidentally fallen into the bath.

l: Eryx, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Eryx was said to be the son of Venus and a famous Sicilian prince. He became king of part of Sicily, founded the city called Eryx on a high hill, and built a temple to Venus there.

l: Venus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Venus was honored at Eryx in a temple founded by Eryx, her son. Eryx, Aeneas, the Sicilians, the Carthaginians, and the Romans all contributed to the temple's offerings and worship.

l: Venus Erycina, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Venus was called Venus Erycina because of her connection with Eryx and the city he founded. Her worship at Eryx continued under the Sicilians, Carthaginians, and Romans, who greatly enriched her temple.

l: temple of Venus at Eryx, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The temple of Venus at Eryx stood on the summit of a high and craggy hill and was richly furnished and adorned with offerings. Daedalus enlarged and fortified the site by building a wall around the summit and making the area level and spacious.

l: Minos's invasion of Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Minos's invasion of Sicily began after he learned that Daedalus had fled there. Minos sailed with a great fleet to the coast of Agrigentum, demanded Daedalus from Cocalus, and was killed during the ensuing encounter.

l: Minos's death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Minos's death occurred when Cocalus kept him in a hot bath until the steam and heat suffocated him. The Cretans buried him with great ceremony in a double sepulchre and established a temple to Venus near the visible upper part.

l: Cretans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The Cretans who accompanied Minos to Sicily buried him after his death. Their ships were later burned by the Sicilians, so they settled in Sicily, where some founded Minoa and others founded Erygum; they later accepted additional Cretans cast upon Sicily after the destruction of Troy.

l: Curetes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The Curetes were goddesses said to have come from Crete to Sicily. They were believed to have secretly raised and concealed Jupiter from Saturn and were honored by the Cretans settled in Sicily and by neighboring peoples.

l: Corybantes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The Corybantes were identified with the Curetes and received worship in Sicily. A temple was built to them by Cretans settled there, and the oracle at Delphi directed many cities to honor them with sacrifices and religious services.

l: temple of the Curetes or Corybantes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The temple of the Curetes or Corybantes was built by Cretans who had settled in Sicily and was richly adorned with gifts. Its stones were brought from the Agyrians over a rough route a hundred furlongs long, and the temple possessed extensive lands and large sacred treasures.

l: Aristaeus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Aristaeus was the son of Apollo and Cyrene and was raised by nymphs, who taught him to curdle milk, make beehives, and plant olive-yards. He married Autonoe and was the father of Actaeon, later helped end a plague on Coos, civilized inhabitants in Sardinia, taught useful practices in Sicily, and learned the rites of the orgia from Bacchus in Thrace. He eventually disappeared near Mount Hiemus and was honored as a god.

l: Apollo, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Apollo fathered Aristaeus with Cyrene. He transported Cyrene to Libya, where the city of Cyrene was later built in her honor, and his oracle at Delphi directed Aristaeus to go to Coos.

l: Cyrene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Cyrene was the beautiful daughter of Hypsaeus and the mother of Aristaeus by Apollo. Apollo carried her to Libya, where a city named Cyrene was later founded after her.

l: Daphnis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Daphnis was said to have been begotten by Mercury upon a nymph in Sicily's Berei Mountains. Raised by nymphs and owner of many herds, he became a skilled shepherd, composer, and inventor of bucolic songs; he also hunted with Diana. After lying with a king's daughter despite a nymph's warning, he lost his sight.

l: Berei Mountains, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The Berei Mountains in Sicily were described as a pleasant region with sweet air, abundant springs, groves of lime and oak, edible roots and bulbs, and many melons. They contained a beautiful valley and a grove dedicated to the nymphs, where Daphnis was said to have been born.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But this concerning Daphnis shall suffice. Now we proceed io .. 99S
s: The unit concerns Orion, described as the biggest and strongest of the heroes and a great hunter who performed notable deeds. He is said to have made the harbour of Acte for Zanclus, from whom Zancle, later Messana and now Messina, took its ancient name. The text discusses traditions about Sicily becoming an island, including the formation of Rhegium, and reports that Orion raised the promontory Pelorus and built a temple to Neptune there. Orion later sailed to Euboea, and his fame was preserved by placing him among the stars.

l: Orion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But this concerning Daphnis shall suffice. Now we proceed io .. 99S
s: Orion is described as the biggest and strongest of all the heroes and as being much given to hunting. For vain glory, he performed many great actions, including making the harbour called Acte for Zanclus and raising the promontory Pelorus, where he built a temple to Neptune. He later sailed to Euboea and resided there.

l: Messana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But this concerning Daphnis shall suffice. Now we proceed io .. 99S
s: Messina is identified as the city formerly called Zancle and afterwards Messana. Its ancient name is connected with Zanclus, the Sicilian king for whom Orion made the harbour called Acte.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But this concerning Daphnis shall suffice. Now we proceed io .. 99S
s: Some ancient writers say that Sicily was once a peninsula and later became an island when the sea cut through its narrowest isthmus. Others attribute the separation to an earthquake, while Hesiod gives a contrary account involving Orion's raising of the promontory Pelorus.

l: Rhegium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But this concerning Daphnis shall suffice. Now we proceed io .. 99S
s: Rhegium was the name given to the place where the narrow neck connecting Sicily to the continent was said to have been severed. Many years later, a city called Rhegium was built there.

l: Orion constellation, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But this concerning Daphnis shall suffice. Now we proceed io .. 99S
s: Orion was fixed as a constellation among the stars in recognition of the glory of his actions. Through this placement, his name became famous for eternity.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: Diodorus Siculus’s Book V begins a description of the islands, starting with Sicily and its ancient peoples, geography, traditions, and religious practices. It recounts traditions linking Sicily with Ceres, Proserpine, Pluto, the first growth of wheat, and the rape of Proserpine at Enna and Syracuse. It describes the Sicanians, Sicilians, Greek colonization of Sicily, the Aeolian Islands and Lipara, and the reputed history of Aeolus. It ends by explaining how the island of Osteodes received its name after Carthaginian mercenaries were abandoned there and died.

l: Diodorus Siculus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: Diodorus Siculus presents Book V as a description of the islands and begins with Sicily, emphasizing orderly historical arrangement and the usefulness of historical writing.

l: Book V, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: Book V begins with Sicily and proceeds to the Aeolian Islands, Lipara, and Osteodes. It discusses geography, origins, religious traditions, peoples, colonization, volcanic activity, and notable events.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: Sicily is described as a large triangular island formerly called Trinacria, Sicania, and finally Sicily. It is associated with Ceres and Proserpine, the first growth of wheat, the rape of Proserpine, and the settlements of Sicanians, Sicilians, and Greeks.

l: Sicanians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: The Sicanians are presented as the first inhabitants of Sicily, although Philistus says they came from Iberia and Timaeus argues that they were indigenous. They originally lived in villages and fortified hill towns, later withdrew westward after volcanic destruction, and fought with the Sicilians until boundaries were established.

l: Sicilians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: The Sicilians are said to have transported themselves from Italy into Sicily after the Sicanians had withdrawn from parts of the island. They expanded into neighboring territories, fought the Sicanians, and later gave their name to the island.

l: Italy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: Italy is identified as the place from which the Sicilians migrated with their families into Sicily. The Aeolian tradition also says that Liparus fled from Italy to the island that later bore his name.

l: Ceres, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: Ceres is associated with Sicily and with the discovery of wheat and the art of husbandry. After Proserpine’s disappearance, she wandered through the world seeking her daughter and gave wheat to hospitable inhabitants, especially the Athenians.

l: Proserpine, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: Proserpine is said to have lived in the meadows of Enna with Ceres and Diana before Pluto carried her away. She is connected with the Sicilian festivals and with the spring and lake called Cyane near Syracuse.

l: Pluto, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: Pluto is said to have carried Proserpine away in a chariot from Sicily and to have descended with her into the underworld through an opening in the earth near Syracuse.

l: wheat, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: Wheat is said to have first grown spontaneously in Sicily, where wild wheat still grew in the territory of Leontium and elsewhere. Ceres later bestowed wheat on peoples who received her kindly, and the Athenians spread its seed to others.

l: Enna, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: Enna is described as lying near a fragrant meadow filled with violets and other flowers. The meadow is presented as the place where Proserpine was carried away, with a cave and underground passage associated with Pluto’s departure.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: Syracuse is associated with the island of Ortygia, the fountain of Arethusa, and the fountain and lake called Cyane. Its inhabitants held annual ceremonies for Ceres and Proserpine and publicly sacrificed bulls by throwing them into the lake.

l: Mount Etna, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: Mount Etna is described as a source of fire and as a place whose eruptions damaged and laid waste to Sicilian territory. Ceres is said to have lit her firebrands at its eruptions while searching for Proserpine.

l: Greeks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: The Greeks were the last major settlers mentioned as colonizing Sicily. They built coastal cities, and their commerce and presence caused the inhabitants to adopt Greek language and ways of living.

l: Aeolian Islands, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: The Aeolian Islands are said to number seven: Strongyle, Euonymos, Didyme, Phoenicusa, Hiera, Ericusa, and Lipara. They lie between Sicily and Italy, are associated with volcanic eruptions, and are connected by tradition with Liparus and Aeolus.

l: Lipara, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: Lipara is the largest named city and island of the Aeolian group in the account, and it was said to have been founded by Liparus. Its inhabitants later shared land, cultivated the islands, defended themselves against Tyrrhenian piracy, and grew wealthy from harbors, baths, fish, fruit, and alum.

l: Aeolus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: Aeolus, identified as the son of Hippotas, arrived at Lipara with companions, married Cyane, and became ruler of the island. He later helped Liparus regain territory in Italy and was honored as a demi-god; tradition also credits him with teaching sailors about sails and forecasting winds.

l: Tyrrhenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: The Tyrrhenians are described as raiders who infested the seas around Lipara. The Liparans built a fleet for defense and later defeated them in several sea battles.

l: Osteodes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: Osteodes is described as a small, uninhabited island west of Lipara. It received its name because approximately six thousand abandoned Carthaginian mercenaries died there, leaving the island filled with their bones.

l: Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: The Carthaginians were engaged in wars with the Syracusans and employed numerous mercenaries. When some mercenaries mutinied over unpaid wages, the Carthaginian senate ordered officers to transport them to Osteodes, where they were abandoned and died.

l: Carthaginian mercenary mutiny, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: The Carthaginian mercenary mutiny began when soldiers were not paid on time and gathered to threaten their commanders and demand their rights by force. The Carthaginian senate responded by secretly ordering their officers to put them to death, leading instead to their abandonment on Osteodes and starvation.

l: rape of Proserpine, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: The rape of Proserpine is said to have occurred in the meadows of Enna, when Pluto carried her away through an underground passage. The account connects the event with Ceres’s grief, the eruption of Mount Etna, famine, and the religious observances of Sicily.

l: Sicilian festivals of Ceres and Proserpine, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: The Sicilians held festivals honoring Ceres and Proserpine in gratitude for receiving wheat first. They celebrated the rape of Proserpine during the wheat harvest and held a ten-day festival for Ceres during wheat sowing, including ritual obscenity intended to make the grieving goddess smile.

l: Greek colonization of Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: Greek colonization of Sicily is described as the final major wave of settlement. Greek settlers built cities on the coasts, and interaction with them led the local inhabitants to adopt Greek language and customs.

l: volcanic eruptions, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. BOOK. V.
s: Volcanic eruptions affected Sicily and the Aeolian Islands, destroying territory and causing the Sicanians to abandon eastern parts of Sicily. Strongyle and Hiera continued to emit vapors, sand, and fiery stones, and some believed underground caverns connected their eruptions with those of Mount Etna.

The Gymnesian islands, also called Baleares, are known for their skilled slingers and distinctive customs. The account then turns to Madeira, a fertile island in the ocean whose discovery is attributed to Phoenician merchants driven there by a storm.

s: Malta lies about eight hundred furlongs from Syracuse and has very good harbours. Its inhabitants are wealthy, practice many crafts including fine-linen weaving, live in stately houses, and are a colony of Phoenicians whose trade made the island famous for wealth and merchandise.

l: Phoenicians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And in this manner these mercenaries (by the fraud of their own .. Having now gone through the i^olides, we shall next view those
s: Phoenicians settled Malta and Gaulus, and founded colonies in Africa and western Europe. Their merchants built Gades and its temple to Hercules, and some were driven by a storm beyond the pillars of Hercules to discover Madeira.

l: Cyrnus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And in this manner these mercenaries (by the fraud of their own .. Having now gone through the i^olides, we shall next view those
s: Cyrnus is the Greek name for the island that the Romans and its natural inhabitants call Corsica. It lies three hundred furlongs from Æthalia, has an easy access and a large harbour called Syracusium, and contains the cities Calaris and Nicaea.

l: Corsica, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And in this manner these mercenaries (by the fraud of their own .. Having now gone through the i^olides, we shall next view those
s: Corsica is a large, mountainous and wooded island with rivers, abundant milk, honey, and flesh, and more than thirty thousand inhabitants. Its people are described as just and humane toward one another, while its inhabitants have a strange language and its bond-slaves are considered especially useful.

l: Sardinia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And in this manner these mercenaries (by the fraud of their own .. Having now gone through the i^olides, we shall next view those
s: Sardinia is described as an island as large as Sicily, inhabited by barbarians called lolaeians. The Carthaginians conquered it but could not enslave the lolaeians, who withdrew into mountain habitations and defended themselves there; the Romans likewise failed to subdue them.

l: lolaeians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And in this manner these mercenaries (by the fraud of their own .. Having now gone through the i^olides, we shall next view those
s: The lolaeians claim descent from people who settled Sardinia with Iolaus and the children of Thespius. They preserved their laws and liberties, and when the Carthaginians and Romans attacked them, they used mountainous terrain and underground caves to resist subjugation.

l: Hercules, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And in this manner these mercenaries (by the fraud of their own .. Having now gone through the i^olides, we shall next view those
s: Hercules is said to have sent children born by the daughters of Thespius, with Iolaus and a large mixed company, to establish settlements in Sardinia. He also instituted celebrated games, and the people of the Gymnesian islands explain their prohibition of silver and gold by recalling his war against Geryon.

l: Iolaus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And in this manner these mercenaries (by the fraud of their own .. Having now gone through the i^olides, we shall next view those
s: Iolaus, described as Hercules's nephew, led the colony sent to Sardinia. He took possession of the island, founded several cities, divided the land, named the people lolaeians after himself, and built public schools, temples, and other useful monuments before returning to Greece.

l: Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And in this manner these mercenaries (by the fraud of their own .. Having now gone through the i^olides, we shall next view those
s: The Carthaginians settled a colony in Pityusa and later conquered Sardinia, although they could not enslave the lolaeians. They also opposed an Etrurian plan to send a colony to Madeira, wishing to retain the island as a possible refuge.

l: Pityusa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And in this manner these mercenaries (by the fraud of their own .. Having now gone through the i^olides, we shall next view those
s: Pityusa lies three days and nights from the pillars of Hercules, one day and night from Africa, and one day's sail from Spain. It is reasonably fruitful, produces fine wool, and contains Eresum, a city inhabited largely by Carthaginians and supplied with strong walls and famous ports.

l: Gymnesian islands, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And in this manner these mercenaries (by the fraud of their own .. Having now gone through the i^olides, we shall next view those
s: The Gymnesian islands lie opposite Spain and are so called because their inhabitants go naked in summer. The greater island is larger than all the islands mentioned except seven, while the lesser is noted for large cattle and mules; both are fertile and together have more than thirty thousand inhabitants.

l: Baleares, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And in this manner these mercenaries (by the fraud of their own .. Having now gone through the i^olides, we shall next view those
s: The islands called Gymnesian by the Greeks are called Baleares by the natives and Romans because of their skill at casting large stones from slings. Their inhabitants are portrayed as expert slingers who use three slings, train from childhood, and can strike armour, shields, and other targets with great force and accuracy.

l: Madeira, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And in this manner these mercenaries (by the fraud of their own .. Having now gone through the i^olides, we shall next view those
s: Madeira is described as a remote, fertile island in the ocean opposite Africa, with mountains, pleasant plains, navigable rivers, gardens, orchards, woods, springs, abundant game and fish, and a mild climate. Phoenician merchants discovered it after a storm drove them far from the African coast, while the Carthaginians later prevented an Etrurian colony from being established there.

l: Great Ocean, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And in this manner these mercenaries (by the fraud of their own .. Having now gone through the i^olides, we shall next view those
s: The ocean lies beyond the pillars of Hercules and contains the remote island described as Madeira. Phoenician merchants entered it after sailing beyond the pillars and were driven into it by a violent storm for many days before reaching the island.
