s: The unit describes Britain, its geography, inhabitants, customs, and political organization, and recounts Julius Caesar's conquest of the island and imposition of tribute on the Britons. It explains that tin is mined in Belerium, carried to Ictis at low tide, and transported by merchants through France toward the river Rhone. It also discusses amber found on Basilea, rejects traditional stories about its origin, and attributes it to the action of the sea and trade.

l: Europe, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, For over against the French shore^ opposite to the Hercynian
s: Europe is described as lying opposite Britain across the ocean, with the Hercynian mountains on the continental shore. The mountains are said to be the greatest in Europe.

l: Britain, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, For over against the French shore^ opposite to the Hercynian
s: Britain is described as the greatest of the islands in the ocean opposite Europe. It is triangular in form, lies obliquely against the continent, has unequal sides, and is said to have a circumference of 42,500 furlongs. Julius Caesar was the first, according to the authors mentioned, to conquer it and compel its inhabitants to pay tribute.

l: Julius Caesar, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, For over against the French shore^ opposite to the Hercynian
s: Julius Caesar is described as the first figure mentioned by an author to have conquered Britain and compelled the Britons to pay tribute. He is said to have lived in the period of the text and to have gained the title of Divine through his achievements.

l: Britons, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, For over against the French shore^ opposite to the Hercynian
s: The Britons are the inhabitants of Britain and are said to have been compelled by Julius Caesar to pay tribute. They are described as using chariots in battle, living in simple cottages, storing ears of grain underground, and being governed by several kings and princes who were generally at peace with one another.

l: Belerium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, For over against the French shore^ opposite to the Hercynian
s: Belerium is a British promontory described as four days' sail from the continent. Its inhabitants are considered more civilised and courteous to strangers because of their dealings with merchants, and they mine and refine tin there.

l: British customs and way of life, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, For over against the French shore^ opposite to the Hercynian
s: The inhabitants of Britain are described as preserving their ancient customs, including the use of chariots in battle. They live in mean cottages covered mainly with reeds or sticks, store grain underground, and make bread from grain they bruise. They are characterized as sincere, honest, content with plain food, and strangers to excess and luxury.

l: tin, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, For over against the French shore^ opposite to the Hercynian
s: Tin is dug from rocky ground in Belerium, where it is mixed with veins of earth. The inhabitants melt and refine it, beat it into four-square pieces, and carry it to Ictis; merchants then transport it through France toward the mouth of the river Rhone.

l: merchants, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, For over against the French shore^ opposite to the Hercynian
s: Merchants trade with the inhabitants of Belerium, whose contact with them is said to make them more civilised and courteous to strangers. The merchants buy tin, transport it from Ictis through France on horses' backs, and carry it toward the river Rhone.

l: Ictis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, For over against the French shore^ opposite to the Hercynian
s: Ictis is described as a British island near Belerium. At low tide, the water between Belerium and Ictis becomes dry, allowing the inhabitants to carry large quantities of tin across in carts.

l: France, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, For over against the French shore^ opposite to the Hercynian
s: France is the route by which merchants carry tin for thirty days' journey on horses' backs toward the mouth of the river Rhone.

l: amber, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, For over against the French shore^ opposite to the Hercynian
s: Amber is described as being cast up by the working of the sea on the island of Basilea and as being transported by the inhabitants to the opposite continent before being brought to the regions of the text. The unit rejects the story that amber comes from the tears of Phaeton's sisters and instead gives precedence to the accounts of faithful historians.

l: Basilea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, For over against the French shore^ opposite to the Hercynian
s: Basilea is an island in the ocean opposite Scythia above Gaul. It is said to contain an abundance of amber cast upon it by the action of the sea, unlike any other part of the world.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, ' After this account given of the western islands, we conceive it not
s: The unit describes Celtica and Gaul, their peoples, geography, resources, customs, warfare, religion, and relations with neighboring nations and Rome. It recounts that Hercules visited Celtica, built Alesia, and fathered Galates, whose name was said to have given rise to Galatians and Gaul. The Gauls are portrayed as tall and warlike, skilled in combat, devoted to gold and imported wine, and guided in religious and political matters by Druids, Bards, and prophets. The unit also describes human sacrifice, including the killing of prisoners and captives as offerings to the gods.

l: Celtica, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, ' After this account given of the western islands, we conceive it not
s: Celtica is presented as the realm where a famous ruler lived and where Hercules built Alesia. The inland peoples beyond Massilia, around the Alps, and on the northern side of the Pyrenees are called Celts, while the peoples farther south are called Gauls, though the Romans generally use the name Gauls for all of them.

l: Hercules, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, ' After this account given of the western islands, we conceive it not
s: Hercules marched into Celtica while engaged in war against Gallia and built Alesia there. He fathered Galates with the daughter of the ruler of Celtica.

l: Gauls, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, ' After this account given of the western islands, we conceive it not
s: The Gauls inhabit a country divided among numerous nations and are described as tall, pale, red-haired, warlike, and skilled in combat. They use chariots, swords, darts, distinctive clothing and armor, and are said to honor gold, entertain strangers, preserve the heads of notable enemies, and believe in the immortality and transmigration of souls.

l: Druids, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, ' After this account given of the western islands, we conceive it not
s: The Druids are philosophers and divines held in great veneration by the Gauls. Sacrifices may not lawfully be offered without a philosopher, and Druids are obeyed in both peace and war; they can also intervene between opposing armies and pacify them.

l: Bards, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, ' After this account given of the western islands, we conceive it not
s: The Bards are poets who sing melodious songs to musical instruments like harps. They praise some people and disparage others, and they are honored and obeyed by the Gauls in peace and war.

l: wine, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, ' After this account given of the western islands, we conceive it not
s: Gaul is said to produce neither wine nor oil because of its excessive cold. Imported wine is eagerly consumed by the Gauls, who are described as drinking it to excess, and Italian merchants exchange wine for high prices, sometimes receiving a boy for a hogshead of wine.

l: gold, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, ' After this account given of the western islands, we conceive it not
s: Gaul is said to have no silver mines but abundant gold carried down from the mountains by rivers. The inhabitants collect, crush, wash, and smelt the gold, using it to make bracelets, chains, rings, and other ornaments; pieces of gold are also scattered in temples, where the Gauls will not touch them.

l: human sacrifice, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, ' After this account given of the western islands, we conceive it not
s: Human sacrifice is practiced among the Gauls in several forms. In divination, a victim is struck with a sword and the manner of the victim's fall, bodily convulsions, and flow of blood are examined; prisoners kept for five years and captives taken in war may also be impaled, burned, or otherwise offered to the gods.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having spoken of the Celts, we shall now give an account of tbck
s: The unit describes the Celtiberians, their origins, customs, weapons, and long resistance to the Romans, and also discusses neighboring Iberian peoples, especially the Vaccaei and Lusitanians. It recounts Iberia’s rich deposits of silver, gold, brass, and tin, the exploitation of its mines, and the wealth gained by Phoenicians, Carthaginians, and Romans. It then describes the harsh conditions and martial habits of the Ligurians before turning to the history, institutions, luxury, and decline of the Tyrrhenians. The account emphasizes how warfare, mining, trade, slavery, and agricultural fertility shaped these peoples and regions.

l: Gauls, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having spoken of the Celts, we shall now give an account of tbck
s: The Celts formerly fought the Iberians over the boundaries of their countries. They eventually agreed to inhabit the same country and intermarry, and their descendants were said to be called Celtiberians.

l: Celtiberians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having spoken of the Celts, we shall now give an account of tbck
s: The Celtiberians arose from the union of Celts and Iberians and became famous because they occupied a rich and fertile country. They fielded strong cavalry and hardy infantry, used several kinds of shields and armor, and carried well-tempered two-edged swords and short daggers. Their customs included washing and cleaning their teeth with urine, showing cruelty to enemies and criminals but hospitality toward strangers, and drinking honey-based beverages as well as purchased wine.

l: Iberians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having spoken of the Celts, we shall now give an account of tbck
s: The Iberians are described as inhabiting a country rich in mines and including peoples such as the Celtiberians and Lusitanians. Young, needy, and courageous Iberians, especially Lusitanians, formed armed groups in the mountains and made raids for wealth, using steep terrain as shelter from larger armies.

l: Romans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having spoken of the Celts, we shall now give an account of tbck
s: The Romans eventually subdued the Celtiberians after long and difficult wars, though they could not completely end the raiding of the Iberians. After Iberia came under Roman control, Italians managed its mines with large numbers of slaves.

l: Lusitanians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having spoken of the Celts, we shall now give an account of tbck
s: The Lusitanians are called the most valiant of the Cimbri and are described as agile fighters who used small, strong shields, iron weapons, swords, helmets, and long-range darts. They performed nimble dances in peacetime, marched to measured rhythms in war, and sang paeans before attacking. Their young and needy men also gathered in mountain bands and raided for wealth.

l: Celtiberian and Lusitanian warfare, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having spoken of the Celts, we shall now give an account of tbck
s: Celtiberian warfare relied on stout cavalry, hardy infantry, large or light shields, rough protective clothing, greaves, helmets with red plumes, and exceptionally sharp two-edged swords. Lusitanian warfare emphasized agility, small shields, hooked iron weapons, accurate darts, and the ability to pursue or escape rapidly. Celtiberian horsemen dismounted after routing an enemy and joined the infantry in combat.

l: Iberia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having spoken of the Celts, we shall now give an account of tbck
s: Iberia is portrayed as a broad, fertile, and mineral-rich country inhabited by several peoples. It contained abundant deposits of silver, gold, brass, and tin, and its mountainous regions enabled raiders to evade large armies.

l: silver mines of Iberia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having spoken of the Celts, we shall now give an account of tbck
s: The silver mines of Iberia were exceptionally rich, with ore found throughout the soil and extracted through deep shafts and underground galleries. Miners diverted underground rivers and used Egyptian pumps, attributed to Archimedes the Syracusan, to drain the workings. The mines generated great wealth first for ordinary miners and later for Italian managers and their owners.

l: Pyrenees, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having spoken of the Celts, we shall now give an account of tbck
s: The Pyrenees divide Gaul from Iberia and Celtiberia, extending from the sea toward the northern ocean. The text says that ancient fires set by shepherds supposedly melted silver ore in the mountains, causing silver to flow out in streams, and connects their name with a Greek word meaning fiery.

l: Phoenicians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having spoken of the Celts, we shall now give an account of tbck
s: The Phoenicians allegedly purchased Iberian silver for trifling exchange goods before the inhabitants understood the value of the metal. They transported the silver to Greece, Asia, and other nations, becoming greatly enriched, and used the wealth to establish colonies in Sicily, nearby islands, Africa, and Sardinia.

l: Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having spoken of the Celts, we shall now give an account of tbck
s: The Carthaginians are said to have opened all the mines when they controlled Spain. Their wealth from the mines enabled them to hire many brave soldiers and wage wars that nearly ruined the Romans, Sicilians, and Africans.

l: Spain, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having spoken of the Celts, we shall now give an account of tbck
s: Spain contained extensive mines and was once controlled by the Carthaginians before coming under Roman control. Tin was also found in many parts of Spain, where it was dug up and melted like gold and silver.

l: silver, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having spoken of the Celts, we shall now give an account of tbck
s: Silver was found in extraordinary abundance in Iberia, sometimes described as flowing from melted ore in the Pyrenees. Phoenician merchants carried it abroad, while later Iberian mining produced immense wealth for Carthaginians, Romans, Italians, mine owners, and merchants.

l: Ligurians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having spoken of the Celts, we shall now give an account of tbck
s: The Ligurians lived in a rough, barren, mountainous, and heavily wooded country, where they worked constantly for little food. Men and women cut trees, broke rocks, hunted, and gathered wild plants; some lived in fields, hollow rocks, or caves. They were lean, sinewy, strong, daring, lightly armed, and willing to sail in small vessels through dangerous seas.

l: Tyrrhenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having spoken of the Celts, we shall now give an account of tbck
s: The Tyrrhenians were formerly powerful warriors who occupied a large country, founded famous cities, maintained a navy, and controlled the sea named after them. They were credited with inventing the trumpet and with giving generals ivory thrones and purple robes. They also studied natural philosophy, especially thunder and lightning, but later became luxurious, drunken, and less warlike.

l: Italy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having spoken of the Celts, we shall now give an account of tbck
s: Italy is described as the region in which the Tyrrhenians lived and as the land whose southwestern sea received the name Tyrrhenian from them. The Romans adopted several Tyrrhenian institutions and architectural practices.

l: Tyrrhenian/Etruscan society, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having spoken of the Celts, we shall now give an account of tbck
s: Tyrrhenian society was marked by fertile land, abundant harvests, elaborate homes, porticoes, fine carpets, silver cups, numerous servants, and richly furnished apartments for servants and freemen. The people were said to have abandoned earlier sobriety for idleness, luxury, drunkenness, and debauchery.

l: mining labor and slavery, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having spoken of the Celts, we shall now give an account of tbck
s: After Roman control began, Italian interests bought many slaves and placed them under mine masters and overseers. The slaves opened shafts, dug galleries, carried ore from deep underground, and worked without rest under compulsion and beatings; many died from overwork, while others regarded death as preferable to continued labor.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The unit describes the islands in the Arabian ocean near Arabia, especially the Holy Island and Panchsea, including their products, government, religious institutions, economy, and legendary history. It then turns to the Aegean islands near Greece, beginning with Samothracia and its traditions concerning an ancient flood, Saon, and the island’s sacred mysteries. The account connects Samothracia with Jupiter, Dardanus, Jasion, Harmonia, Cadmus, Cybele, Ceres, and the gods associated with initiation. It also describes the marriage of Cadmus and Harmonia and the spread of religious rites from Samothracia to other places.

l: Arabian ocean, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The southern islands lying in the Arabian ocean are described as being east of Arabia, near Gredosia. The account later contrasts these islands with those in the Aegean sea near Greece.

l: Holy Island, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The Holy Island lies near the utmost point of Arabia, and it is unlawful to bury the dead there. It produces abundant frankincense, myrrh, and other odoriferous spices.

l: Panchsea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Panchsea is described as a large, fertile island with cities, vineyards, palms, walnut trees, wild beasts, mines, and abundant wine. Its inhabitants are divided into priests and artificers, husbandmen, and militia and shepherds; the priests govern the island and distribute its common produce.

l: Panchaeans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The Panchaeans inhabit the sacred island and transport its myrrh and frankincense to Arabian merchants. They are one of the three peoples associated with Triphylius Olympus.

l: Cretans (in Panchsea), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Cretans are among the strangers who dwell in Panchsea. The priests claim that they originally came from Crete and preserve words of the Cretan speech, which they offer as evidence of their ancient connection.

l: Panara, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Panara is a wealthy and grand city in Panchsea. Its citizens are called the suppliants of Jupiter Triphylius and govern themselves democratically, choosing annual presidents while referring matters of life and death and important affairs to the priests.

l: Jupiter Triphylius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Jupiter Triphylius is worshipped in Panchsea, where his temple is held in great veneration. The citizens of Panara call themselves his suppliants.

l: Panchean priests, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The Panchean priests govern Panchsea, judge controversies, control public affairs, and distribute the common revenues and produce according to need and merit. They receive a double proportion, serve the gods, wear elaborate robes and ornaments, and are forbidden to leave the consecrated ground.

l: temple of Jupiter Triphylius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The temple stands about sixty furlongs from Panara in a fertile plain and is built of white marble with large pillars, statues, priestly apartments, and valuable sacred objects. Its grounds include gardens, fountains, a river called the water of the sun, and land consecrated to the gods.

l: frankincense, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Frankincense grows abundantly on the Holy Island and is used for the worship of the gods throughout the world. It comes from a small tree whose bark yields drops like tears when cut.

l: myrrh, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Myrrh grows on the Holy Island and flows forth when the earth around the roots of its tree is dug up. Trees in rich soil produce it twice a year, with the spring myrrh deep red and the later myrrh white.

l: Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The islands in the Aegean sea near Greece are introduced after the account of the islands near Arabia. Samothracia is the first of these islands to be described.

l: Samothracia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Samothracia was said to have been formerly called Samos and to have received its later name from colonies from Samos and Thrace. Its inhabitants preserve an ancient speech and religious traditions, and the island is associated with a great flood, Saon, and sacred mysteries.

l: Samothracians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The Samothracians report that their island experienced a great flood before any other nation. They say that survivors escaped to higher ground, were delivered from danger after appealing to the gods, and marked the places of their preservation with boundaries and altars.

l: Samothracian flood, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The Samothracian flood is said to have entered through the mouth of the Cynele and through the Hellespont after the Pontic sea overflowed. It submerged much of the island’s low country, and fishermen later brought up stone pillar-heads that were taken as evidence of drowned cities.

l: Saon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Saon gathered the scattered inhabitants of Samothracia into one body, made laws, and divided them into five tribes named after his sons. He is variously described as the son of Jupiter and Nympha or of Mercury and Rhena.

l: Jupiter, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Jupiter is named as the father of Saon in one account and as the father of Dardanus, Jasion, and Harmonia with Electra. He revealed the sacred mysteries to Jasion and is said to have initiated strangers into them.

l: Mercury, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Mercury is named as the alternative father of Saon, with Rhena as Saon’s mother in that account. He gave Jasion a harp at the marriage of Cadmus and Harmonia and was said to have written sacred inscriptions in Panchsea.

l: Dardanus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Dardanus, a child of Jupiter and Electra, left Samothracia for Asia in a pinnace. He built the city of Dardanus, established the kingdom of Troy, gave his name to the Dardanians, and was said to have settled Dardanians above Thrace.

l: Jasion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Jasion, a child of Jupiter and Electra, received the sacred mysteries from Jupiter. He married Cybele, was said to have been received among the gods, and received rich gifts of corn from Ceres.

l: Harmonia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Harmonia, a child of Jupiter and Electra, married Cadmus in a marriage celebrated in the presence of the gods. She was the sister of Jasion.

l: sacred Samothracian mysteries, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The sacred Samothracian mysteries were ancient rites observed on Samothracia and newly revived in the account. They could not ordinarily be heard by the uninitiated, but Jupiter was said to have revealed them to Jasion and to have initiated strangers.

l: Cadmus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Cadmus, the son of Agenor, came to Samothracia while seeking Europa and was initiated into its sacred mysteries. He married Harmonia and later built Thebes in Boeotia as commanded by an oracle.

l: Cybele, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Cybele married Jasion and bore Corybas. She later travelled with Dardanus and Corybas to Phrygia, where the sacred mysteries of the mother of the gods were brought into Asia.

l: Ceres, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Ceres was said to have been in love with Jasion and gave him corn at the marriage of Cadmus and Harmonia. The account says that the story of Pluto as the son of Jasion and Ceres arose from these gifts.

l: gods of the Samothracian mysteries, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The gods of the Samothracian mysteries were believed to be present and to help those who had been initiated and called upon them in sudden danger. Initiates were also believed to become more pious, righteous, and good, and several famous heroes were said to have prospered in war through their favor.

l: great mother of the gods, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The great mother of the gods had sacred mysteries that were taught by Electra to Jasion and later brought into Asia by Dardanus, Cybele, and Corybas. Corybas gave his name to those who celebrated these rites in a state of religious frenzy.

l: marriage of Cadmus and Harmonia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The marriage of Cadmus and Harmonia was celebrated in the presence of the gods and was described as the first marriage so celebrated. Ceres, Mercury, Minerva, Electra, Apollo, and the other gods were said to have provided gifts, instruction, music, and joyful acclamations.

l: initiation into the sacred mysteries, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Initiation into the sacred mysteries was originally restricted to those permitted to hear the rites, but Jupiter was said to have initiated strangers. Cadmus was initiated at Samothracia, and initiation was believed to bring divine assistance, piety, righteousness, and success in war.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now finished what concerns Samothracia, the course of
s: The unit recounts the early history of Naxus, formerly called Strongyle, beginning with the settlement of the Thracians under Butes. After the Thracians were expelled by Otus and Ephialtes, the island was called Dia until the Carians, led by King Naxus, renamed it after him. It also describes Theseus leaving Ariadne on Naxus after a vision of Bacchus, and the Naxians’ traditions about Bacchus’s upbringing and favor toward their island. The account concludes by describing the first inhabitants of Syme.

l: Naxus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now finished what concerns Samothracia, the course of
s: Naxus was formerly called Strongyle and was first settled by the Thracians. After the Thracians left and the Carians took possession of the island, their king Naxus ordered that it be named Naxus after himself.

l: Strongyle, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now finished what concerns Samothracia, the course of
s: Strongyle was the former name of Naxus. Butes and other Thracians settled there, practiced piracy, and held the island for more than two hundred years before drought and famine forced them to leave.

l: Thracians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now finished what concerns Samothracia, the course of
s: The Thracians first settled Strongyle under Butes and seized the island, later carrying off women from other places. They were eventually defeated and expelled by Otus and Ephialtes, and drought and famine had already compelled them to leave the island after more than two hundred years of occupation.

l: Butes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now finished what concerns Samothracia, the course of
s: Butes, the younger son of Boreas, plotted to murder his brother and was sent away with his accomplices. He led Thracians to Strongyle and engaged in piracy, but after seizing and ravishing Coronides, he was driven mad by Bacchus and died by casting himself into a pit.

l: Bacchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now finished what concerns Samothracia, the course of
s: Bacchus caused Butes to become mad after Butes dishonored Coronides. He was said to have been brought forth in Naxus and entrusted to nymphs there, and the Naxians believed that his upbringing caused him to favor their island. He appeared to Theseus in a vision, led Ariadne away, and was credited by the Naxians with aiding them and enriching their island.

l: Agassamenus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now finished what concerns Samothracia, the course of
s: Agassamenus was made king of Strongyle after Butes. He married Pancratis and gave her mother, Iphimedia, to one of his intimate friends, whom he appointed general of his army.

l: Pancratis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now finished what concerns Samothracia, the course of
s: Pancratis, the daughter of Aloeus, was carried away to Strongyle by the Thracians. Agassamenus married her after Sicuius and Hecaterus fought over her, and she later died.

l: Otus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now finished what concerns Samothracia, the course of
s: Otus, sent by Aloeus to find Iphimedia and Pancratis, invaded Strongyle with Ephialtes. They defeated the Thracians, captured the city, later took possession of the island, expelled the Thracians, and renamed it Dia. Otus and Ephialtes subsequently fought one another and died in the battle.

l: Ephialtes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now finished what concerns Samothracia, the course of
s: Ephialtes joined Otus in invading Strongyle to recover Iphimedia and Pancratis. The brothers defeated and expelled the Thracians, renamed the island Dia, and later killed one another in battle; the inhabitants afterward worshiped them as demi-gods.

l: Theseus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now finished what concerns Samothracia, the course of
s: Theseus came from Crete to the island with Ariadne and landed there. In his sleep he saw Bacchus threatening him with ruin unless he abandoned Ariadne, so he left her and withdrew from the island.

l: Ariadne, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now finished what concerns Samothracia, the course of
s: Ariadne arrived on the island with Theseus. After Theseus abandoned her because of a vision involving Bacchus, Bacchus led her at night to Mount Arius and then disappeared; Ariadne was not seen afterward.

l: Naxians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now finished what concerns Samothracia, the course of
s: The Naxians preserved many stories about Bacchus, claiming that he was raised among them and that their island was especially loved by him. They attributed their wealth, power, fleet, successes against the barbarians, and excellent wine to his favor.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Nireus, the son of Charops and Aglaia, was, in after times^
s: The unit recounts the legendary origins and later settlements of Rhodes, its inhabitants, and the neighboring Chersonesus. It describes the Telchines, Neptune, Rhode, Jupiter, Sol, and the Heliades, including floods, divine punishments, migrations, and the development of arts and astrology. It also explains the division of Rhodes among Lindus, Ialysus, and Camirus, and recounts the activities of Triopas in Caria and Chersonesus. The unit concludes with the story of Hemithea and the fame of her healing temple at Castabus.

l: Rhodians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Nireus, the son of Charops and Aglaia, was, in after times^
s: The Rhodians regarded Rhodes as consecrated to Sol and worshipped the sun above all other gods, believing him to be the ancestor from whom they sprang. They later received Phorbas as a proprietor, and after his death honored him as a demi-god; they also honored Althasmenes as a demi-god.

l: Rhodes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Nireus, the son of Charops and Aglaia, was, in after times^
s: Rhodes was first inhabited by the Telchines and was later associated with Rhode, the daughter of Neptune and Halia. The island was said to have suffered a great inundation, after which Sol cleared it, and it was later divided among Lindus, Ialysus, and Camirus.

l: Telchines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Nireus, the son of Charops and Aglaia, was, in after times^
s: The Telchines were said to have inhabited Rhodes, invented several useful arts, and made some of the first statues of the gods. They were also reputed to practice magic, raise storms, transform themselves, and envy those who learned their arts; foreseeing an inundation, they abandoned Rhodes and dispersed.

l: Neptune, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Nireus, the son of Charops and Aglaia, was, in after times^
s: Neptune was brought up by the Telchines and Caphira, the daughter of Oceanus, after being entrusted to their care by Rhea. He loved Halia and fathered six sons and a daughter, Rhode; after his sons committed outrages under Venus's influence, he buried them beneath the earth.

l: Rhode, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Nireus, the son of Charops and Aglaia, was, in after times^
s: Rhode was the daughter of Neptune and Halia. Sol was said to have loved her and to have named the island Rhodes after her.

l: Jupiter, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Nireus, the son of Charops and Aglaia, was, in after times^
s: Jupiter was said to have conquered the Titans and to have fathered Spartaeus, Cronius, and Cytus by the nymph Hamalia. His sons were among those preserved by fleeing to higher ground during the inundation of Rhodes.

l: Heliades, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Nireus, the son of Charops and Aglaia, was, in after times^
s: The Heliades were the seven sons of Sol and Rhode: Ochimus, Cercaphus, Macir, Actis, Tenages, Triopas, and Daedalus. They were credited with excellence in learning, astrology, navigation, and the division of the day into hours; after Tenages was murdered by his brothers, the principal perpetrators and their accomplices fled.

l: Sol, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Nireus, the son of Charops and Aglaia, was, in after times^
s: Sol was said to have loved Rhode, named Rhodes after her, and cleared the island after its inundation. The account also explains the myth by saying that the sun dried the island's original mud and moisture, making it productive of living creatures and giving rise to the Heliades.

l: Triopas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Nireus, the son of Charops and Aglaia, was, in after times^
s: Triopas, one of the sons of Sol and Rhode, fled after killing his brother and later went to Thessaly, where he helped expel the Pelasgians. He then went to Caria and built Triopium, and afterward gained Chersonesus and much of the adjoining Carian country.

l: Lindus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Nireus, the son of Charops and Aglaia, was, in after times^
s: Lindus was one of the three sons of Cercaphus who jointly ruled Rhodes. He shared in dividing the country and built a city that was called Lindus after him.

l: Ialysus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Nireus, the son of Charops and Aglaia, was, in after times^
s: Ialysus was one of the three sons of Cercaphus who jointly ruled Rhodes. He shared in dividing the country and built a city that was called Ialysus after him.

l: Camirus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Nireus, the son of Charops and Aglaia, was, in after times^
s: Camirus was one of the three sons of Cercaphus who jointly ruled Rhodes. He shared in dividing the country and built a city that was called Camirus after him; later, Althasmenes and his followers settled in Camirus.

l: Chersonesus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Nireus, the son of Charops and Aglaia, was, in after times^
s: Chersonesus was described as a region opposite Rhodes, named either for its shape or for an earlier petty prince. The Curetes expelled the Cares from it and divided it into five parts, while Cyrnus and Triopas later established power there.

l: Caria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Nireus, the son of Charops and Aglaia, was, in after times^
s: Caria was associated with Chersonesus and was partly ruled by Cyrnus after he settled there while searching for Io. Triopas later built Triopium in Caria and gained Chersonesus together with much of the adjoining country.

l: Hemithea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Nireus, the son of Charops and Aglaia, was, in after times^
s: Hemithea was the name given to Molpadia, one of the daughters of Staphylus and Chrysothemides, after Apollo brought her safely to Castabus. She was honored by the Chersonesians for her revelations and was believed to heal the sick and safely deliver women in childbirth.

l: temple of Hemithea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Nireus, the son of Charops and Aglaia, was, in after times^
s: The temple of Hemithea at Castabus became famous and attracted inhabitants and strangers with sacrifices and gifts. It was said to have been spared by the Persians when they destroyed other temples and by thieves, and its mysteries included offerings of water and honey while excluding anyone who had touched or eaten swine.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: The unit concerns Crete, its earliest inhabitants, and the origins and deeds attributed to the Idæi Dactyli, Curetes, Titans, and numerous gods. It describes how these figures introduced useful arts, including fire-making, metalworking, agriculture, navigation, laws, justice, crafts, letters, and poetry. It recounts the upbringing and reign of Jupiter, his benefits to mankind, and his wars against the giants. It also explains the origins and functions attributed to Ceres, Proserpina, Pluto, Neptune, Minerva, the Muses, and other deities.

l: Crete, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Crete is said to have been first inhabited by the Eteocretæ and later by the Idæi Dactyli, Curetes, and Titans. Its traditions identify many useful discoveries and the births or activities of numerous gods with the island.

l: Idæi Dactyli, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: The Idæi Dactyli were regarded as the first recorded inhabitants of Crete, dwelling on Mount Ida; some traditions instead derive them from Mount Ida in Phrygia. They were credited with magic, sacred rites, the use of fire, and the discovery and working of iron and brass, and one of them was called Hercules, who instituted the Olympic games.

l: Curetes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Nine Curetes followed the Idæi Dactyli, dwelling in mountains, caves, and beneath trees. They were credited with managing flocks, taming cattle, gathering honey, hunting, making darts, swords, and helmets, organizing communities, and inventing armed dancing; their noise concealed Jupiter from Saturn while they raised him.

l: Titans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: The Titans were said to be contemporary with the Curetes and to dwell near Gnossus in Crete. Their number and parentage were disputed, but they were credited with useful inventions and included Saturn, Hyperion, Rhea, Themis, Mnemosyne, and others.

l: Saturn, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Saturn, the eldest Titan, obtained the kingdom and brought his subjects from barbarism toward a more civilized life. He was associated with justice, integrity, prosperity, and the blessed conditions of the age in which he reigned; some traditions say he killed his children because an oracle warned that Jupiter would overthrow him.

l: Hyperion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Hyperion was said to have first discovered the motions of the sun, moon, and other stars, together with the seasons and divisions of time. He was therefore called the father of the planets because he taught others their knowledge and nature.

l: Rhea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Rhea was one of the Titans and the mother of Jupiter. Grieved by Saturn's destruction of their children, she hid Jupiter on Ida and entrusted him to the Curetes and nymphs for protection and upbringing.

l: Themis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Themis was credited with teaching divination, sacred rites, and laws for the worship of the gods and the preservation of peace and good government among men. Terms for those who preserve sacred laws and for giving oracles were connected with her name and practice.

l: Mnemosyne, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Mnemosyne was said to have discovered logic and assigned proper names to things so that discourse could be clearly understood. She was also credited with whatever assisted human memory.

l: Prometheus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Prometheus was said to be the son of Japetus. Although some claimed that he stole fire from the gods for mankind, the account says that he found the method of striking fire from flint or stone.

l: Ceres, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Ceres was credited with discovering seed-corn and teaching people how to sow, house, and bake it. After Proserpina's birth and abduction by Pluto, she burned the corn in her grief, but after recovering her daughter she gave seed-corn to Triptolemus; she was also said to have established laws for just and truthful conduct.

l: Proserpina, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Proserpina was the daughter of Ceres and was carried off by Pluto. Her abduction caused Ceres to grieve and burn the corn, and her recovery led Ceres to reconcile with Jupiter and distribute seed-corn through Triptolemus.

l: Pluto, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Pluto was said to have first introduced sepulchres and splendid funerals, which led to his being regarded as lord of the dead and ruler of the infernal shades. He also carried off Proserpina.

l: Neptune, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Neptune was said to have first practiced navigation, equipped a navy, and served as admiral under Saturn. He was also credited with managing horses and teaching horsemanship, for which he was called Hippius.

l: Jupiter, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Jupiter was hidden on Ida by Rhea and raised by the Curetes and nymphs on milk, honey, and the milk of the goat Amalthea. After succeeding Saturn, he promoted justice, lawful courts, peace, and good government, punished violent and impious persons, established communities, and was credited with ruling the heavens and storms; he also fought the giants.

l: Ida, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Ida was the Cretan mountain associated with the Idæi Dactyli and the upbringing of Jupiter. Its cave was said to have concealed Jupiter, and the surrounding places were consecrated to him.

l: Minerva, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Minerva was said to have been born in Crete at the sources of the river Triton, where a chapel stood in her honor. Jupiter entrusted her with the cultivation of olive trees and the extraction of oil, and she was also credited with garments, architecture, pipes, wind music, and tools for handicrafts.

l: Muses, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: The Muses were credited by some with inventing letters and composing verses called poetry. Others attributed the invention of letters to the Syrians, saying that the Phoenicians altered their form and transmitted them to the Grecians.

l: agriculture, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Agriculture is chiefly represented through Ceres's discovery and teaching of seed-corn, sowing, housing, and baking. The account also records competing claims by Egyptians, Athenians, and Sicilians concerning where corn was first discovered or introduced.

l: laws and courts of justice, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Law and justice are attributed to Saturn, Themis, Ceres, and Jupiter in different ways. Saturn promoted integrity, Themis taught laws and sacred order, Ceres was said to establish rules for truthful dealings, and Jupiter instituted punishment for injuries and the orderly settlement of disputes in courts.

l: war against the giants, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Jupiter fought giants because of their violence, oppression, and refusal to submit to justice. He was said to have killed Mytinus in Crete and Typhon in Phrygia, and later fought giants at Pallene in Macedonia and at Phlegra, identified with the plains near Cumæ; those who fought with the gods were destroyed.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Vulcan, they say, found out the working of iron, brass, silver, and
s: The unit describes traditions concerning the Cretan gods, heroes, rulers, and the origins of Crete and neighboring islands. Apollo, Hercules, Diana, Ceres, Jupiter, and Europa are associated with divine ancestry, inventions, travels, or worship. It recounts how Minos and Rhadamanthus ruled Crete and extended their influence across islands and Asian coasts. It also narrates the settlement of Lesbos, the activities of Macareus, the origins of the Cyclades, and the later expansion of the Greeks.

l: Apollo, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Vulcan, they say, found out the working of iron, brass, silver, and
s: Apollo is credited with inventing the harp and its kind of music, discovering physic, and teaching the use of the bow. He instructed Asculapius in physic, and the Cretans delighted in shooting, calling the bow Scythicus. He was said to have been born in Crete and was associated with Delos, Lycia, and Delphos.

l: Hercules, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Vulcan, they say, found out the working of iron, brass, silver, and

The elder Hercules traveled through the whole world, punished the wicked, destroyed wild beasts, delivered people from bondage, and remained unconquered and invulnerable. s: Diana was closely associated with Dictynna, and some thought them to be the same person. She was honored in Crete and was said to have been born there, while also being associated with Ephesus, Pontus, Persia, and other places.

He possessed a great fleet, conquered many islands, and was the first of the Greeks to gain dominion of the seas. He was renowned for justice and valor, later died in Sicily while warring against Cocalus, and was made a judge of hell alongside Rhadamanthus.

s: Ceres was said to be the mother of Pluto and to have sailed to Attica, Sicily, and Egypt. She delivered corn and taught the inhabitants of those places how to sow it, after which she was highly honored.

s: Europa was the daughter of Agenor and the mother, by Jupiter, of Minos and Rhadamanthus. She was reportedly carried into Crete on the back of a bull through the providence of the gods.

He gained several islands and parts of the Asian coast, appointed rulers over territories, and was later regarded as a judge of hell with Minos.

s: Macareus, the son of Crinacus and descendant of Jupiter, settled Lesbos after the island had been laid waste. He gathered Ionians and people from other nations, ruled justly, divided lands among his followers, and sent colonies to Chios, Samos, Cos, and Rhodes.

s: The Cyclades were formerly desolate and uninhabited until Minos sent Cretan colonies to many of them, divided their lands, and subdued much of the neighboring Asian coast. After the destruction of Troy, the Carians took control of some islands and shared others with the Cretan inhabitants, but the Greeks later expelled them from most of the Cyclades.
